episode_title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us

stories.summary: Luca Cavalli-Sforza, born around 1918, started his career studying blood groups to learn about the deep past. In the early 1960s — decades before the human genome was sequenced (which only happened in 2001) — he made what looked like an insane bet: that human history would be uncovered through the genetic trails of human beings. The science finally caught up around the turn of the century, and now ancient DNA has rewritten what we know about prehistory.
stories.insight: A reminder that the most important scientific bets are placed long before the technology to vindicate them exists. Vision in science is the ability to commit to a measurement framework that won't be possible for decades.

stories.topic: Mitochondrial Eve and the Great Khichri
stories.summary: Mitochondrial DNA studies in the 1980s established that all of humanity descends from one woman in Africa, called mitochondrial Eve. After 'a few moments of pleasure,' she eventually wrought 7.5 billion descendants. Full-genome sequencing revealed that Europe had five major migrations, India had four, and 3-5% of European and Asian genomes are actually Neanderthal — meaning we were 'having a party with Neanderthals about 50 to 60,000 years ago.'
stories.insight: The story of humanity is not separate races slowly diverging, but constant intermingling. The 'Neanderthal' pejorative ironically describes part of who we all are — racial purity is a fiction that the genetic data has decisively destroyed.

stories.summary: Drawing on Peggy Mohan's Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: Sanskrit is not a pure Indo-European language. It contains retroflex sounds — where the tongue touches the roof of the mouth, as in the difference between 'tal' and 'taal' — that don't exist in Persian or other Indo-European languages just to the west. Those retroflex sounds came from the Dravidian languages the Aryan migrants encountered. The Sanskrit of the Vedas is therefore a delightful mix of imported Indo-European and absorbed local tongues. This happened because migrant men married local women, raising boys who spoke their mothers' language until early childhood ended and they shifted to the men's language.
stories.insight: Pure cultural origins are largely a myth: the most 'sacred' classical languages are themselves products of intermingling. The mechanism is intimate — language travels through mothers in cradles, not just through conquerors on horses.

stories.topic: Caste Endogamy Is Real and Recent
stories.summary: For about 2,000 years after the Aryan migration (roughly 1900 BCE to 100 CE), the Indian subcontinent was a 'great party' of intermixing — no caste, no in-group/out-group lines visible in the genetic data. Around 100 CE, a particular ideological strand in the Gangetic belt won out and severe caste endogamy began, leaving a clear genetic signature. David Reich's line: 'India is many thousands of small populations.' Upper-caste men were also more successful at spreading their genes than lower-caste men.
stories.insight: Caste endogamy is the deepest sin of Hinduism, but not its original sin — it is roughly 2,000 years old, while the subcontinent's intermingling is 4,000 years old. What is recent and constructed can also be reversed.

stories.topic: The British State Legibility Project Created Caste
stories.summary: When the British arrived, they encountered a society they couldn't possibly grok. Their early interlocutors were Brahmin elites who sold them the four-varna narrative from the Vedas and Manusmriti. The British, needing to measure the country, made everyone tick a box for caste and religion. By Soros's principle of 'reflexivity,' the act of categorisation changed the category — millions of tribals were forced to tick 'Hindu' and only now are asserting prior identities. Both narratives — that caste was a British construct and that genetic data shows it was real — contain truth.
stories.insight: Measurement is never neutral: forcing people to write down their identity has a Heisenberg effect, ossifying what was multitudinous. Two seemingly contradictory truths can both hold — caste was real, AND the British exacerbated and froze it.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh Did More for Dalits Than Almost Anyone
stories.summary: The 1991 reforms brought hundreds of millions of Dalits out of poverty, a fact rarely noted. Amit argues that Manmohan Singh did more for Dalits than any other thinker of the twentieth century — even while recognising Ambedkar's greatness. The Dalit activist Chandra Bhan Prasad once said his two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.
stories.insight: Liberalisation and markets do real, often-uncelebrated work in dismantling old hierarchies. The most effective Dalit emancipator may have been the economist who unleashed growth, not just the politicians who fought directly against caste.

stories.summary: Twenty-five years ago, Amit had a Standard Chartered credit card. Being Bengali and lazy, he never set up auto-pay and waited for the bank to call him. Once the outstanding was so trivial — Rs. 80 — that they didn't bother calling, and his card was revoked silently. The Rs. 80 ballooned with interest to Rs. 29,000. He refused on principle to pay it, even though he easily could. To this day his CIBIL score is 'shit,' even though he pays vendors in advance and has never been late on anything that mattered.
stories.insight: Traditional credit scores often miss the actual person. Holistic data — the kind that smartphones already collect — can build a far more accurate picture of creditworthiness than any single number reflecting one ancient dispute over Rs. 80.

stories.summary: An older friend who travelled through Europe and the Soviet Union playing chess in the 1980s once told Ajay the standard road hack: when your underwear gets dirty, wear it inside out. Every underwear is effectively two underwear. Ajay declined to delve deeper into what this does to the gene pant in question. The same friend, the legend goes, once 'traded his corduroy for sex in Russia.'
stories.insight: A glimpse of the texture of Soviet-era travel and improvisation. Also a comic illustration of why a 'male underwear index' would have been very different in shortage economies — the elasticity of underwear demand depends on the rest of the consumption basket.

stories.summary: In 2009, Tom Diamond visited his brother Alex, who worked at a satellite imagery firm. Alex had just used satellite data to verify a factory's inventory for a sale. Sitting around afterward doing rock versions of Schubert on guitar, the brothers remembered Sam Walton's old line — that he gauged Walmart's quarter by counting cars in the parking lot. They asked: what if we did this for every store? Alex quit, bought three years of imagery, back-tested it on Walmart, and found stark correlations between parking traffic and quarterly results. They founded RS Metrics. Two Berkeley professors later showed that parking-lot data across 67,000 stores would have given investors a 4.7% edge over the standard investor — an extraordinary number in a world that fights for 0.2%.
stories.insight: Big breakthroughs often come from cross-pollination during play — two musicians noodling on Schubert recombined an old Walton anecdote with new satellite data. The lesson for finance and beyond: what looks like 'digital exhaust' or 'unused imagery' is often the next alpha.

stories.summary: A few years ago, a train carrying 268 bogies of iron ore had an accident and capsized. The market reacted predictably — stocks crashed, iron-ore prices spiked. But traders looking at satellite imagery saw that the iron ore was actually just lying flat on the ground and would be easy to reload. They correctly bet that the market would recover faster than consensus expected and made a killing.
stories.insight: Markets price the assumed worst case; remote sensing prices reality. The edge belongs to whoever measures the situation directly rather than reasoning from headlines.

stories.topic: Reading Oil Tanks From Their Shadows
stories.summary: Many large oil tanks have a floating roof that sits on top of the oil and falls as the oil is consumed. From overhead satellite imagery, when the tank is full there is no shadow inside it; as the tank empties, the floating roof drops and casts a shadow whose size — given a known sun position — reveals exactly how much oil is left.
stories.insight: Geometry plus a satellite is enough to know a private inventory the owner thinks is hidden. The deeper point: as soon as a phenomenon throws any kind of shadow into the public domain, it can be measured.

stories.topic: The Lipstick Index, Counterintuitive in COVID
stories.summary: Leonard Lauder of Estee Lauder noticed in 2001 that lipstick sales went up after the recession. His theory: in tough times, people stop buying $200 handbags but still want to feel luxurious, so they buy a $20 lipstick — the cheapest accessible luxury. The lipstick index correctly tracked the 2008 and 2011 downturns. But COVID broke it: people were wearing masks, so why bother with lipstick?
stories.insight: Behavioural indices encode an unstated assumption — here, that there is a face for the lipstick to be seen on. When the underlying ritual is suspended, the index breaks. Always ask what an index implicitly assumes about its world.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here: Ancient DNA and the New Science of the Human Past
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Reich's book on what full-genome sequencing has revealed about human prehistory.
recommendations.reason: The definitive account of how ancient-DNA evidence has overturned the older archaeological consensus. Reich's line that 'India is many thousands of small populations' is the empirical bedrock for understanding caste endogamy as a measurable, datable phenomenon.

recommendations.item: Early Indians: The Story of Our Ancestors and Where We Came From
recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Joseph's accessible synthesis of the genetic evidence about India's four major migrations.
recommendations.reason: The book that translates Reich's findings to the Indian context — first Indians, the Harappans, ancient North and ancient South Indians, the Aryan migration. Tony Joseph also appeared on The Seen and the Unseen for a deeper conversation.

recommendations.item: Tony Joseph on The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Amit's long-form conversation with Tony Joseph.
recommendations.reason: The audio companion to Early Indians — a detailed walk through the four migration waves and the science of ancient DNA.

recommendations.item: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Peggy Mohan's linguistic forensics on how Indian languages evolved.
recommendations.reason: Source of the stunning insight that Sanskrit is itself a khichri — that retroflex sounds came from the Dravidian languages the Aryans encountered, not from the Indo-European languages they brought. Mohan does for language what Reich does for genes.

recommendations.item: Peggy Mohan on The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Amit's deep conversation with Peggy Mohan.
recommendations.reason: The long-form discussion of language as a forensic tool for reconstructing history — including the role of mothers and child-language in transmitting and transforming tongues.

recommendations.item: A History of Hinduism (Episode 76 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier EIE episode on Hinduism.
recommendations.reason: Builds on Manu Pillai's framing of Hinduism as something far more open and assimilative than the Brahminical narrative the British inherited — context for why caste and religion in India had different historical paths.

recommendations.item: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
recommendations.creator: Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Pillai's book on how modern Hindu identity was constructed.
recommendations.reason: Source of the introductory chapter Amit calls 'A Brief History of Hinduism,' which frames Hinduism as an open-source religion that absorbed local practices for two millennia — quite at odds with the rigid caste system running parallel to it.

recommendations.item: The Hindi Heartland
recommendations.creator: Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: Wahab's book on the Hindi belt.
recommendations.reason: Contains the key excerpt on tribals being forced into the 'Hindu' box during British censuses, and the contemporary mass movement of those communities reasserting their pre-categorisation identities. A live demonstration of state legibility's reflexivity effect.

recommendations.item: Caste and the Census (Episode 417 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: An episode on the politics and history of caste enumeration.
recommendations.reason: Deeper treatment of the argument that classifying castes through the census is itself a force that ossifies them — relevant to ongoing debates about the modern caste census.

recommendations.item: The Alchemy of Finance
recommendations.creator: George Soros
recommendations.context: Soros's book on financial markets.
recommendations.reason: Source of the concept of reflexivity — the idea that the narratives we impose on a system change how the system behaves. Amit applies it to caste here, but it originated as a theory of finance.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with the Dalit activist.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Chandra Bhan Prasad named his two heroes as Ambedkar and Adam Smith — the encapsulation of Amit's argument that markets and liberalisation have done real work for Dalit emancipation.

recommendations.item: In Praise of Floods
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's late book on the ecology of pre-agricultural diversity.
recommendations.reason: The source of the staggering homogenisation statistics: of 200,000 plant varieties, only twelve dominate the food chain; of 60,000 animals, only four (goats, sheep, pigs, cows). Amit notes parts are masterpiece, parts are flawed, but reading anything by Scott is worthwhile.

recommendations.item: Against the Grain
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's earlier book on the dark side of the agricultural revolution.
recommendations.reason: The argument that the agricultural age brought havoc on humankind — diversity collapsed, hierarchy and disease and slavery rose. Essential context for understanding why diversity (in genes, languages, crops, peoples) is always and everywhere good.

recommendations.item: Stage.in
recommendations.creator: Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: A 'Netflix for Bharat' platform that streams content in Indian dialects.
recommendations.reason: A live counter-example to the great flattening: a market-empowered service that monetises Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and other dialects at Netflix prices. Markets first homogenise (chase scale) then re-diversify (empower the long tail).

recommendations.item: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with the founder of Stage.
recommendations.reason: The long-form story behind Stage.in and the case for dialect-language media as a market opportunity, not a charity.

recommendations.item: On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints
recommendations.creator: Tobias Berg, Valentin Burg, Ana Gombovic and Manju Puri
recommendations.context: The 2018 FDIC working paper on alternative credit scoring using digital data.
recommendations.reason: The German-data study quoted in the episode — that iPhone users default less than Android users, that typos in email addresses predict default, that 2 a.m. shoppers are riskier. The empirical foundation for digital-exhaust credit scoring.

recommendations.item: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Episode 116 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous week's EIE episode on satellite night-light data of Russia.
recommendations.reason: The companion piece to this one — both episodes argue that new measurement opens up phenomena previously locked away from us. The Russia episode is the prequel; this one extends the same logic to genes, phones and parking lots.

recommendations.item: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
recommendations.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The XKDR paper analysing the Russia-Ukraine war using nighttime light data.
recommendations.reason: The applied-research artefact behind Episode 116 — a worked example of how satellite measurements give independent observers leverage that traditional government statistics cannot.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier EIE episode on population.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's argument that fertility is sensitive to the mood of a nation — when authoritarianism rises, people have fewer children. Amit invokes it here while wondering whether the hemline index is just the same phenomenon dressed differently.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's policy book.
recommendations.reason: Linked in the episode notes; the foundational reference for Ajay's repeated emphasis that measurement is the bedrock of all knowledge and that India's data infrastructure is profoundly under-invested.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons (course)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their newly launched online course at lifelessons.co.in.
recommendations.reason: Their joint distillation of the ideas they've taught, written about and debated for decades, packaged as a course for general audiences.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course.
recommendations.reason: A standing recommendation from the show notes for anyone wanting to write more clearly — Amit's signature pedagogical project.

recommendations.item: The India Uncut Newsletter
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack newsletter.
recommendations.reason: Where Amit publishes the columns and essays that often surface in EIE episodes.

recommendations.item: The LEAP Blog
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and collaborators
recommendations.context: The blog of the LEAP project.
recommendations.reason: Where much of the empirical and policy work Ajay references is written up — including measurement-driven analyses of the Indian economy.

core_ideas.concept: Measurement Is the Bedrock of Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: The journey of knowledge runs from Kepler to Newton: measurement first, then statistical regularities in the data, then theory. Without data, you have nothing — only conversation, only the trading of opinions. India in particular suffers from chronic under-measurement, and the great institutional measurement systems (CSO, CMIE) were until recently the only game in town. The last twenty years have brought a measurement revolution: nighttime lights, ancient DNA, digital exhaust, satellite imagery — new eyes that see things old institutions never could.
core_ideas.quote: If you don't have the data, you don't have anything. Then it's just conversation.

core_ideas.explanation: We look back on 19th-century medicine — bloodletting, no germ theory, hospitals more lethal than home — and laugh at how primitive it was. We assume our current knowledge is more or less the truth. But two centuries from now, people will look back on us the same way. Genome sequencing has just overturned a century of confident archaeology; what we hold dear today is tomorrow's bloodletting.
core_ideas.quote: Two centuries later, we will look back on the people of 2025 and think those poor sods knew nothing.

core_ideas.explanation: We did not branch out of Africa into separate, stable populations. The genetic record shows constant intermingling: Europe had five major migrations, India four, Latin America four. 3-5% of European and Asian DNA is Neanderthal. Linguistic data tells the same story — Sanskrit itself absorbed retroflex sounds from local Dravidian tongues. The dominant fact of human history is mixture; racial purity is a fiction the data has decisively destroyed.
core_ideas.quote: We are all fundamentally one people, we are all a khichri.

core_ideas.concept: The Naturalistic Fallacy and Hume's Is-Ought
core_ideas.explanation: When we observe genuine biological or cultural differences between groups, the temptation is to derive a 'should' from the 'is.' But G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and Hume's is-ought distinction warn against this. Differences exist, differences should be celebrated — but they should never become the ground for racial hierarchy or stereotype. What is natural is not, by virtue of being natural, right.
core_ideas.quote: Differences are amazing. Differences should be celebrated. But the differences are not a problem.

core_ideas.concept: Caste Endogamy as a Measurable, Datable Phenomenon
core_ideas.explanation: For 2,000 years after the Aryan migration, the subcontinent was a great party of intermixing — no caste signature in the genes. Around 100 CE, severe caste endogamy began, and the genetic record now lights up clearly: India is many thousands of small reproductively isolated populations rather than one large one. The endogamy implies control of female sexuality, which implies sexual repression and the prudish morality that survived Victorian overlay into the present.
core_ideas.quote: If you're looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese — they're a large population. India is many thousands of small populations. — David Reich

core_ideas.explanation: Borrowed from Soros (in finance) and James C. Scott (in politics): the act of measurement changes the thing being measured. When the British forced Indians to tick a single box for caste or religion, they did not merely record an existing reality — they ossified what had been multitudinous. Scott's Seeing Like a State could equally be subtitled State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences. The Heisenberg effect is not just for physics.
core_ideas.quote: Shining a light on the phenomenon changes the phenomenon.

core_ideas.concept: Diversity Is Always and Everywhere Good
core_ideas.explanation: From James C. Scott: of 200,000 plant varieties, only twelve dominate our food chain; of 60,000 animals, only four. There are now three chickens on Earth for every human, all industrially farmed. The same homogenisation has happened to languages, where dialects vanish under hegemonic state-languages — 'a language is a dialect with an army.' Markets initially homogenise (chasing scale) but eventually empower the long tail (Stage.in for Bharat dialects). Diversity in genes, crops, languages and ideas is the precondition of resilience.
core_ideas.quote: For every human being on this planet there are three chickens.

core_ideas.explanation: The phrase 'digital exhaust' captures the residue of normal life — emails, purchases, battery levels, recharge frequency, contact lists, typing speed. Companies like Smart Finance, Tala and Lendo turn this exhaust into credit scores. They don't impose prior beliefs (e.g. 'low battery means risky') — machine learning surfaces correlations from millions of phones and assigns weightages no human told it to. The black box knows things its makers don't.
core_ideas.quote: We are leading our normal life... and as a side effect there is this digital exhaust of information that you might otherwise consider to be just trash.

core_ideas.concept: Privacy Threats Run Upside Down in India
core_ideas.explanation: India has its privacy framework backward: the government has unlimited access to personal information while restricting private firms. The state can coerce; Google cannot. The primordial requirement for a privacy regime is to limit the government's gaze, not the corporation's — yet Indian privacy law focuses on the second and ignores the first.
core_ideas.quote: If there is need for protection, it is against the state.

core_ideas.concept: Triangulation and the Updation of Priors
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's lifelong methodological commitment: any phenomenon should be measured through multiple independent data sources to test whether they agree. Convergence boosts confidence; divergence forces investigation. All measurement ultimately exists to update priors — weak data shifts priors weakly, strong data shifts them strongly. Knowing the strength and limits of your sources is more important than the data itself.
core_ideas.quote: All this is ultimately about updation of our priors.

core_ideas.concept: Behavioural Indices and Their Hidden Assumptions
core_ideas.explanation: Lipstick (cheapest accessible luxury rises in downturns), male underwear (delayed in downturns), hemline (rises with prosperity), tie (falls with layoffs), diaper rash (sales of ointment rise as parents skimp on diapers), stripper club traffic, billion prices (online prices as proxy for inflation). Each index is a creative angle on consumer behaviour. But each carries hidden assumptions — the lipstick index broke during COVID because masks suspended the underlying ritual of being seen. Always ask what an index implicitly assumes about its world.
core_ideas.quote: People are wearing masks, so they don't need lipstick.

core_ideas.concept: The Billion Prices Project and Independent Inflation Measurement
core_ideas.explanation: Roberto Rigobon and Alberto Cavallo built the Billion Prices Project by scraping massive volumes of online price data and constructing alternative inflation indices. Two key findings: online prices closely correlate with offline prices, and between 2007-2015 in Argentina, official inflation claimed 7-10% while their data showed 20-30%. The crisis was real, the official numbers were lies, and remote measurement caught it.
core_ideas.quote: We are measuring an economy with a small amount of data, but we have access to a lot more — so why don't we use that?

core_ideas.explanation: When alternative-data investors gain a 4.7% edge from satellite imagery, some object to the unfairness. Ajay's response: the function of finance is to recruit many smart people to produce and aggregate information, and the resulting prices are a public good — they make the economy work better. Speculative trading is voluntary; nobody asks small investors to play. People who don't have the resources should buy index funds and hold. Investor protection should not collapse into speculator protection.
core_ideas.quote: If it's too hot, then leave the kitchen.

core_ideas.explanation: Hannah Arendt's observation that fertility tracks the mood of a nation: people have more children when the world feels good and fewer when it feels bleak. Recent claims suggest China's population may be considerably smaller than its official figures. The hemline index — rising in roaring times, falling in depressions — may be one more behavioural reflection of the same underlying phenomenon: when life feels good, people feel sexy, exuberant and hopeful enough to commit.
core_ideas.quote: Authoritarians run out of people to oppress. — Hannah Arendt

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens by mistakenly calling Amit 'Omitvarma'; Amit retorts: 'I'm not Omit, I'm Amit for you. Yeah. Just as you are Ajay and not Ajoy. Two can play this game.'

Amit on the destination of knowledge: 'The road to knowledge begins with data, and the road to knowledge ends in despair, but leaving that aside — once you get the knowledge you realize what the world is really like.'

Amit on mitochondrial Eve: '...all seven and a half billion of us. And you laugh? This is a serious subject. But I suspect the lady would also laugh if she knew what she had wrought — all for a few moments of pleasure.'
Amit on the persistent Neanderthal slur: 'people will often use Neanderthal as a pejorative — Ajay is a Neanderthal, what will he understand of art? Actually that's part of who we are.'

Ajay's underwear-in-Soviet-Union story about an unnamed elder chess-traveler friend who would wear his underwear inside out on day two ('every underwear is effectively two underwear') — and who once 'traded his corduroy for sex in Russia.'
Amit on his CIBIL score: 'My CIBIL credit score went to hell... and yet I fancy that if you could see all the other data about me, you would realize that I am an absolutely upstanding citizen.'

Amit on Greenspan's male underwear index: 'the amount of time between buying underwear is — pun not intended — stretched, and therefore you delay it as far as possible — till the elastic is falling off completely.'
Amit calling indexes plural sexier than indices: 'we do not talk of the sisses, we talk of the sexes.'

Ajay opening on smartphones: 'I have never seen you without your smartphone, Ajaisha. Always, always you are sending messages on your smartphone... and you always say while you blush, I am checking the weather. I'm not so sure about that.' (Amit is teasing Ajay back.)

Amit's parting joke about T-shirts: he's at 0.5 out of 10 on the EIE shorts index because of his all-black phase, while Ajay is at 9.5. He suggests launching a parallel site 'Turn White' for non-black-wearers.
Mitochondrial Eve — the single African woman from whom mitochondrial DNA suggests all living humans descend, established by 1980s mitochondrial-DNA studies.
Wittgenstein: 'It is impossible to contribute all of the world because we are limited by language' — invoked to argue that different languages encode different ways of feeling and thinking.
G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and David Hume's is-ought distinction — invoked to warn against turning observed differences (between groups, sexes) into prescriptions about how things should be.
George Soros's concept of 'reflexivity' from The Alchemy of Finance — applied here to caste: the act of categorising changes the categorised, just as market narratives change market reality.
James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State — invoked through Ajay's quip that an alternative title would be 'State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences.'
Sam Walton's old quip about gauging Walmart's quarter by counting cars in the parking lot — the seed-anecdote for satellite-imagery alternative-data finance.
Leonard Lauder's coinage of the 'lipstick index' in 2001 — the cheapest accessible luxury rises during recessions.
Alan Greenspan's 'male underwear index' — Greenspan also famously argued that better measurement, not more theory, was where the marginal gains in economics lay.
Hannah Arendt: 'Authoritarians run out of people to oppress' — invoked to link the politics of repression to declining fertility.

AlphaZero in chess — invoked as a parallel for digital-exhaust ML credit scoring: the algorithm makes accurate predictions whose internal reasoning humans must reverse-engineer afterward (e.g. realising AlphaZero valued initiative more than material).
China's 'social credit system' — invoked as the creepy state-coerced mirror of the voluntary, market-based alt-data scoring done by firms like Smart Finance and Tala.

Javier Milei — referenced in the context of Argentine inflation; the Billion Prices Project's data showed real inflation at 20-30% while official figures claimed 7-10%, foreshadowing the crisis Milei now governs through.
